steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on History Gradient Update (HGU), a more stable optimization method for diffusion-based inverse problem solvers that also works with latent diffusion models on small datasets. Cover the problem setup, the gaps in prior solvers, our contributions and a short summary of results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Inverse problems and the need for good priors
- Problem 1: GD optimization of the data fidelity term is unstable
- Problem 2: pixel-based diffusion solvers need large-scale data
- Our method and contributions
- Results summary

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Inverse problems
  - recover missing data from sparse measurement {\bm{y}}; formulation with data-fidelity + prior term
  - \left|\left|{\mathcal{A}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\right|\right|_{2}^{2}: data fidelity, consistent with measurements
  - \lambda R\left({\bm{x}}\right): prior, realistic, follows ground truth distribution p\left({\bm{x}}\right)
  - sparsity of {\bm{y}} -> ill-posed -> need good priors
  - pre-trained generative priors: GANs, VAEs, diffusion models
- Optimization instability
  - prior diffusion solvers use basic Gradient Descent (GD) on data fidelity term
  - loss-guided optimization is stochastic, naturally unstable
  - GD only uses gradient of a single step
  - -> hard to optimize, inaccurate samples
  - fix: historical gradient information -> more stable, high quality
  - not yet explored; no evidence of convergence properties of GD for data fidelity
- Data scale
  - pixel-based diffusion models widely used for inverse problems; good priors, iterative optimization
  - accurate prior from large-scale data, inaccurate from small-scale
  - limits data-constrained tasks e.g. medical image inverse problems
  - no previous work on small-scale datasets
- Our method
  - new optimization method, expands applicability
  - (1) prove evidence of convergence properties of GD
  - (2) History Gradient Update (HGU): historical gradient from previous steps adaptively adjusts sample-level gradient -> stable, better samples
  - (3) latent diffusion model (LDM) in solver -> accurate prior from small-scale data
- Results
  - HGU + LDMs beat SOTA supervised and unsupervised methods on small-scale medical datasets
  - extended to natural image restoration, competitive with SOTA zero-shot methods
  - any modality regardless of dataset scale; use available LDMs like Stable Diffusion
  - Fig. 1 visual results

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Solving inverse problems is very important, since it usually means recovering missing data from a sparse measurement {\bm{y}}, which is usually formulated as:

where \left|\left|{\mathcal{A}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\right|\right|_{2}^{2} is the data-fidelity term, which makes sure the reconstructed results are consistent with the measurements, and \lambda R\left({\bm{x}}\right) is a prior term, which makes sure the reconstructed results are realistic and follow the ground truth image distribution p\left({\bm{x}}\right). Because {\bm{y}} is sparse, these solving processes are well-known ill-posed problems. So it is important to use good prior models to get high-quality results. Pre-trained generative models are commonly used as the prior models, including GANs, VAEs, and diffusion models.

Previous research on the optimization in diffusion-based inverse problem solvers, specifically optimizing the data fidelity term, has used the most basic Gradient Descent (GD) strategy to get the generated result. But the loss-guided optimization of the data fidelity term is usually a stochastic process and it is naturally unstable. Also, the GD strategy only relies on the gradient in a single step to optimize the target. Because of this the current diffusion-based solvers are difficult to optimize and in the end they produce inaccurate samples. One solution is to put historical gradient information into the optimization processes, which can make them more stable and give high-quality samples. However current research has not explored the historical gradient information yet, and no studies have given evidence of the convergence properties of the GD strategy when optimizing the data fidelity term.

- pixel-based diffusion models widely used for inverse problems; good priors, high-quality samples in iterative framework
- but: accurate prior from large-scale data, inaccurate from small-scale -> limits data-constrained tasks e.g. medical image inverse problems
- no previous work on small-scale datasets
- our method: (1) prove convergence evidence for GD; (2) History Gradient Update (HGU): historical gradient adaptively adjusts sample-level gradient, stabilizes, better samples; (3) LDM in the solver -> accurate prior from small-scale data
- results: HGU + LDMs beat SOTA supervised/unsupervised on small-scale medical datasets; natural image restoration competitive with SOTA zero-shot; any modality, any dataset scale, use LDMs like Stable Diffusion; Fig. 1 visuals

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Solving inverse problems is very important, since it usually means recovering missing data from a sparse measurement {\bm{y}}, which is usually formulated as:

where \left|\left|{\mathcal{A}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\right|\right|_{2}^{2} is the data-fidelity term, which makes sure the reconstructed results are consistent with the measurements, and \lambda R\left({\bm{x}}\right) is a prior term, which makes sure the reconstructed results are realistic and follow the ground truth image distribution p\left({\bm{x}}\right). Because {\bm{y}} is sparse, these solving processes are well-known ill-posed problems. So it is important to use good prior models to get high-quality results. Pre-trained generative models are commonly used as the prior models, including GANs, VAEs, and diffusion models.

Previous research on the optimization in diffusion-based inverse problem solvers, specifically optimizing the data fidelity term, has used the most basic Gradient Descent (GD) strategy to get the generated result. But the loss-guided optimization of the data fidelity term is usually a stochastic process and it is naturally unstable. Also, the GD strategy only relies on the gradient in a single step to optimize the target. Because of this the current diffusion-based solvers are difficult to optimize and in the end they produce inaccurate samples. One solution is to put historical gradient information into the optimization processes, which can make them more stable and give high-quality samples. However current research has not explored the historical gradient information yet, and no studies have given evidence of the convergence properties of the GD strategy when optimizing the data fidelity term.

Recent research has widely used pixel-based diffusion models to solve inverse problems. These models work well as prior models and can generate high-quality samples in an iterative optimization framework. But they have a significant limitation: they learn accurate prior information from large-scale data, but inaccurate prior information from small-scale data. This limits how efficient and applicable they are for data-constrained tasks, like medical image inverse problems. As far as we know, no previous work has looked at whether diffusion-based solvers apply to small-scale datasets.

In this paper we try to address these issues by introducing a new optimization method, which greatly expands the applicability of diffusion-based solvers. Specifically, (1) to address the optimization problems in diffusion-based solvers, we prove the evidence of the convergence properties of the GD strategy. (2) Based on this evidence, we develop a new strategy for optimizing the data fidelity term, called History Gradient Update (HGU), which uses the historical gradient from previous optimization steps to adaptively adjust the sample-level gradient. This stabilizes the whole optimization process and improves the quality of the final samples. (3) We introduce the latent diffusion model (LDM) to the diffusion-based solver, so that we can learn accurate prior information from small-scale data.

Extensive experiments on various inverse problems show that HGU with LDMs outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised methods on small-scale medical datasets. Also, since it is a general method for inverse problem solvers, we extend HGU to the natural image restoration task, and there HGU gets competitive performance compared to other state-of-the-art zero-shot methods. HGU gives a valuable optimization tool for solving the inverse problem. It allows the community to solve the inverse problem for different modalities regardless of the scale of the dataset, and to use the vast amount of available LDMs such as Stable Diffusion. Fig. 1 shows some representative visual results of the proposed method.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Inverse problem solving is of great significance, as it typically involves recovering missing data from sparse measurement {\bm{y}}, which is usually formulated as:

where \left|\left|{\mathcal{A}}{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\right|\right|_{2}^{2} is the data-fidelity term that ensures the reconstructed results are consistent with the measurements, and \lambda R\left({\bm{x}}\right) is a prior term that ensures the reconstructed results are realistic and follow the ground truth image distribution p\left({\bm{x}}\right). Due to the sparsity of {\bm{y}}, the solving processes are well-known ill-posed problems. It is therefore important to take advantage of good prior models to generate high-quality results. Pre-trained generative models are commonly used as the prior models, including GANs [1,2], VAEs [1,3], and diffusion models [4,5,6].

Previous research on the optimization in diffusion-based inverse problem solvers, specifically on optimizing the data fidelity term, has traditionally used the most basic Gradient Descent (GD) strategy [5,7,8,9] to obtain the generated result. However, the loss-guided optimization of the data fidelity term is typically a stochastic process that is naturally unstable. In addition, the GD strategy relies only on the gradient in a single step to optimize the target. These facts make current diffusion-based solvers difficult to optimize and ultimately lead to inaccurate samples. One solution is to incorporate historical gradient information into the optimization processes, which can make them more stable and produce high-quality samples. However, current research has yet to explore historical gradient information, and no studies have provided evidence of the convergence properties of the GD strategy when optimizing the data fidelity term.

Pixel-based diffusion models have been widely used to solve inverse problems in recent research [10,6,8,11,5,12,9]. These models can effectively act as prior models and generate high-quality samples in an iterative optimization framework. However, they have a significant limitation: they can learn accurate prior information from large-scale data, but not from small-scale data. This limits their efficiency and applicability to data-constrained tasks, such as medical image inverse problems. To the best of our knowledge, no previous work has investigated the applicability of diffusion-based solvers on small-scale datasets.

In this paper, we address the above issues by introducing a new optimization method that greatly expands the applicability of diffusion-based solvers. Specifically, (1) to address the optimization problems within diffusion-based solvers, we prove the evidence of the convergence properties of the GD strategy. (2) Based on this evidence, we develop a new strategy for optimizing the data fidelity term, namely History Gradient Update (HGU), which uses the historical gradient from previous optimization steps to adaptively adjust the sample-level gradient, stabilizing the whole optimization process and improving the quality of the final samples. (3) We introduce the latent diffusion model (LDM) to the diffusion-based solver so that we can learn accurate prior information from small-scale data.

Extensive experiments on various inverse problems demonstrate that HGU with LDMs outperforms state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised methods on small-scale medical datasets. Additionally, as a general method for inverse problem solvers, HGU is extended to the natural image restoration task, where it achieves competitive performance compared to other state-of-the-art zero-shot methods. HGU provides a valuable optimization tool for solving the inverse problem, allowing the community to solve it for different modalities regardless of the scale of the dataset and to leverage the vast amount of available LDMs such as Stable Diffusion. Fig. 1 shows some representative visual results of the proposed method.
